rv.q: Jamie Lloyd delivers an effortlessly deft revival of Lucy Prebble’s play, set during the clinical trial of a new antidepressant
Slyly updated, the play has not only kept up with the conversations around mental health and depression but, in an era facing unprecedented ontological challenges from digital tech, expanded them.
Jamie Lloyd's exhilarating production... Prebble writes razor-edged dialogue that thinly slices her characters' brains.
His production of The Effect is unfailingly exciting.
The Effect evokes the deliciously unsettling feeling that all of us are nothing more than bundles of chemicals in ongoing experiments.

The Effect is still entirely worth reviving as a showcase for this stellar cast, as a conversation starter about psychiatry’s limitations, and as a love story with the kind of sparky, flashy chemistry that doctors of yore could only dream of.
In all it's a very clever play, definitely worth seeing, but it's terribly brainy.
The Effect is fascinating — but never soul-stirring.
A decade on, Jamie Lloyd directs a revival which, although stylish, has lost some of its efficacy in the intervening years.
The Effect should have a far greater effect than it does.
It’s also just a knockout human drama.

The result is a rivetingly intelligent evening, set by Soutra Gilmour on a traverse stage that splits the Lyttelton in two, suddenly transforming its tricky proscenium arched stage into a thrilling space of exploration.
But despite its imperfections the decision to revive The Effect is a laudable one.
The story grinds towards a lamely predictable conclusion after two long hours.

cn.t: Lloyd's slick revival of Prebble's cerebral 2012 play about love, depression, and clinical trials proves intellectually intense and visually striking, though some find it overly clinical. Critics praise the sharp writing and bold staging.
